title: The Problem With Project-Based Learning
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with a vivid personal story about a student named Seth, whose genuinely independent, imperfect science-fair rocket project lost to polished, clearly adult-assisted entries, and uses it to argue that adult involvement in project-based learning is a widespread problem that is simultaneously unfair, dishonest, and discriminatory against students who do their own work. He argues the harm cuts both ways: students who do the work themselves get no recognition and internalize that effort doesn't matter or that competitions are 'rigged,' while students whose parents or teachers effectively complete the work for them get undeserved credit but privately know they didn't earn it, which he argues can damage self-worth and discourage them from attempting independent work in the future. His proposed fix is a six-point set of concrete guidelines for teachers: teach process skills like the scientific method thoroughly before assigning independent projects, require genuine independent creation with only clarifying-question-level parent involvement, be willing to dock points or require redos for adult-assisted or copied work, limit available materials to what the classroom provides, hold to a pre-shared rubric without grade inflation, and require multiple presentation formats to expose non-student work. He frames protecting project integrity as a matter of honoring students over convenience, reputation, or outward polish.
points: Adult-assisted project work is framed as unfair, dishonest, and discriminatory against students who complete work independently.
Students who genuinely do their own work but go unrecognized can internalize that effort doesn't matter or that competitions are rigged against them.

Provides a six-point guideline set: teach process skills thoroughly first, require independent creation, dock points or require redos for adult-assisted work, limit materials to what's classroom-provided, hold a strict pre-shared rubric, and require multiple presentation formats.
Requiring several presentation formats (written, oral, video, etc.) is specifically recommended as a way to expose work that wasn't actually done by the student.
quotes: It was a brilliant look at how weather affected the performance of different sizes and configurations of rockets he’d made in his garage.
You see, Seth did the project all by himself. And it showed. His tri-fold display board had all the earmarks of a nine-year-old boy—uneven scissor cuts, finger smudges, and remnants of crusted glue.

Presumably, the winning students did help with their projects. But amid all the attention they got that evening—the proud smiles, applause, photos, and balloons—it was hard not to be discouraged. The whole affair was farcical.
Allowing anyone other than students to play an active role in project-based learning is a bad idea. It’s unfair. It’s dishonest. It’s discriminatory toward students who do the work themselves.
Furthermore, they know they didn’t actually do the work, which can destroy their self-worth and leave them afraid to try anything on their own.

Be willing to disallow, require a redo, or remove points for any part of a project that was clearly done by an adult or pulled right off the internet. If you observe the work closely, and look out for it, it’s easy to tell.
You best honor your students not with a meaningless, unearned certificate destined for a box in the family attic, but with skills and abilities that continue to impact them far into the future.
